passages.t: The ark on a new cart, and Uzzah
passages.happening:
David gathers thirty thousand chosen men and sets out for Baale of Judah to bring up the ark of God, called by the name of the LORD of Hosts, ‘who is enthroned between the cherubim that are on it’ (verse 2). They set the ark on a new cart and bring it from the house of Abinadab. His sons Uzzah and Ahio guide the cart. David and all Israel celebrate before the LORD with every kind of instrument (verse 5).

‘When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark of God, because the oxen had stumbled. And the anger of the LORD burned against Uzzah, and God struck him down on the spot for his irreverence, and he died there beside the ark of God’ (verses 6-7).

David is angry that the LORD has burst out against Uzzah, and he names the place Perez-uzzah. He is afraid too: “How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?” (verse 9). So he leaves it at the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. It stays there three months, ‘and the LORD blessed him and all his household’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
David has united the tribes and taken Jerusalem. Now he wants his capital to be the place of the LORD's presence. The ark had been neglected in a private house at Kiriath-jearim, called Baale of Judah here, ever since the Philistines sent it back in Samuel's day (1 Samuel 7:1-2). It lay some eight or nine miles west of Jerusalem. This is probably early in David's reign there, around the beginning of the tenth century BC.

The ark was a wooden chest covered with gold, made at Sinai, holding the tablets of the law. Its lid was flanked by two golden cherubim, winged guardian figures, and Israel spoke of the LORD as enthroned between them. It was the holiest object in Israel. The law said it was to be carried on poles by Levites of the family of Kohath, who must not touch the holy things or they would die. Moving it on a new cart copied the way the Philistines had sent it back (1 Samuel 6:7-8).

The verb for the LORD bursting out is the one used in chapter 5, when he burst out against the Philistines at Baal-perazim. The power that broke through for Israel is the same power, and it is holy.

Obed-edom is called a Gittite, which usually means a man from Gath. Some think it may mean Gath-rimmon, a town given to the Levites. The ark that killed Uzzah brings good to Obed-edom's whole house.
passages.later:
The law had been plain: ‘But they must not touch the holy objects, or they will die’ (Numbers 4:15). Chronicles tells the same story and puts the lesson in David's mouth: “It was because you Levites were not with us the first time that the LORD our God burst forth in anger against us. For we did not consult Him about the proper order” (1 Chronicles 15:13).

The Bible tells of such sudden judgments at other beginnings: Nadab and Abihu on the first day of Israel's worship (Leviticus 10:1-2), and Ananias and Sapphira at the start of the church (Acts 5). They are rare, and they are never presented as God's usual way with his people.
passages.hard:
Why did God kill Uzzah, who was only trying to keep the ark from falling?

Few passages trouble readers more. Uzzah's act seems natural, even helpful. Several answers have been offered in good faith.

One answer stresses that the whole procession ignored clear commands. The ark was to be carried on poles by Levites and never touched, and the new cart copied the Philistines instead of obeying God's instructions, as Chronicles says plainly. Uzzah's family had kept the ark for years and may have grown too familiar with it.

A second answer looks at the word the text uses, irreverence (its exact meaning in Hebrew is uncertain). On this reading Uzzah treated the ark as an object that needed human protection, as if God could not keep his own throne from falling.

A third answer looks at the moment. Just as the ark is about to become the centerpiece of the king's capital, God shows that he will not be used as a political symbol.

None of these answers removes the shock, and David himself is angry and afraid. The chapter does not ask a reader to feel comfortable. It asks a reader to take God's holiness seriously. And it shows the other side too: the same ark brings good to Obed-edom's household, and it does come to Jerusalem once it is carried in the way God gave.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: David's first attempt was sincere and joyful, and it ignored what God had said. Ask where good intentions have led you to worship God on your own terms. And ask how you hold together a God who is near and a God who is holy.

passages.t: The ark comes up with dancing
passages.happening:
David is told, ‘The LORD has blessed the house of Obed-edom and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God’ (verse 12), and he goes to bring it up to the City of David with rejoicing. This time it is carried. ‘When those carrying the ark of the LORD had advanced six paces, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened calf’ (verse 13).

‘And David, wearing a linen ephod, danced with all his might before the LORD, while he and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and the sounding of the ram’s horn’ (verses 14-15).

They set the ark in its place inside the tent David has pitched for it, and David offers burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then ‘he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of Hosts’ (verse 18), and he gives every man and woman a loaf of bread, a date cake and a raisin cake (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The second attempt is different from the first. The ark is carried, not carted, and the procession stops for sacrifice after six steps. David has learned the lesson of Uzzah.

The word for David's dancing, whirling, appears only in this chapter in the whole Old Testament. It suggests energetic, spinning movement. ‘With all his might’ means his whole body and strength were in it. Dancing was a normal part of Israel's worship and of its celebrations of victory.

David wears a linen ephod, a simple priestly garment, instead of royal robes. He leads the worship as a servant of the LORD, not as a king on display. The ram's horn, the shofar, which signaled the troops at Gibeon (2:28), now sounds for the ark.

The gifts of bread, date cake and raisin cake were festival food, and a sign of the king's generosity to his whole people, women as well as men. The move joins the throne of David to the throne of God. The true king of Israel, the chapter is saying, is the LORD, enthroned between the cherubim, and David's city is now his dwelling place.
passages.later:
Chronicles says that this time ‘the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded in accordance with the word of the LORD’ (1 Chronicles 15:15).

A psalm remembers David's zeal for the ark and sings of its coming to rest: ‘Arise, O LORD, to Your resting place, You and the ark of Your strength’ (Psalm 132:8). Another calls God's people to ‘praise His name with dancing’ (Psalm 149:3).
passages.asks: David danced before the LORD with all his might and did not care how he looked. Ask what keeps your own worship guarded. And ask whether you have learned from a failure the way David learned from Uzzah, or only moved on from it.

passages.happening:
‘As soon as David returned home to bless his own household, Saul’s daughter Michal came out to meet him’ (verse 20). She had watched from a window as the ark came in, seen the king leaping and dancing, ‘and she despised him in her heart’ (verse 16). “How the king of Israel has distinguished himself today!” she said. “He has uncovered himself today in the sight of the maidservants of his subjects, like a vulgar person would do” (verse 20).

David answers, “I was dancing before the LORD, who chose me over your father and all his house when He appointed me ruler over the LORD’s people Israel. I will celebrate before the LORD, and I will humiliate and humble myself even more than this. Yet I will be honored by the maidservants of whom you have spoken” (verses 21-22).

‘And Michal the daughter of Saul had no children to the day of her death’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Michal is called Saul's daughter here, not David's wife, and the title points to what divides them. Her complaint is that the king has made himself common. He set aside his royal dress, danced in a priest's linen garment, and showed himself before the servant girls. To her, a king should keep his dignity.

The quarrel plays on two opposite Hebrew words. One means to be heavy, and so to be honored; it is the root of the word for glory. The other means to be light, and so to be lightly esteemed. Michal says, with scorn, that the king has made himself heavy today by making himself cheap. David answers that he will make himself lighter still before the LORD, and that the servant girls she despises will honor him. He chooses to be light in his own eyes, so that God may be weighty.

David also reminds her, sharply, that the LORD chose him over her father's house. The bitterness between Saul's house and David's has not gone away.

The last verse is spare. Michal had no children to the day of her death. The text does not say why, and it is wise not to guess. The verse closes the door on any king from Saul's line through her. It records no word of her own grief.
passages.later: Chronicles tells the same moment in almost the same words: ‘Saul’s daughter Michal looked down from a window and saw King David dancing and celebrating, and she despised him in her heart’ (1 Chronicles 15:29).
passages.asks: Michal cared about the king's dignity, and David cared about God's honor. Ask whose good opinion you are most afraid of losing. And ask what it would cost you to be lighter in your own eyes before God.
